subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Psychology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: 'Prevalence' of mental health problems means:
options: How common a disorder is in a population
questions.explain: Prevalence refers to how widespread or common a mental health problem is within a population.

questions.q: According to the AQA specification, the reported prevalence of mental health problems has generally:
questions.explain: Reported prevalence has increased, partly due to better recognition, reduced stigma and changes in modern living.

questions.q: Which is a likely reason MORE people are now diagnosed with mental health problems?
options: Reduced stigma so more people seek help
questions.explain: Reduced stigma and greater awareness mean more people seek help and are diagnosed, raising reported prevalence.

questions.q: Which is an example of an effect of mental health problems on society?
questions.explain: Effects on society include costs to healthcare, lost working days and pressure on services and families.

questions.q: Which is a common characteristic (symptom) of depression?
options: Low mood and loss of interest or pleasure
questions.explain: Depression is marked by persistent low mood and loss of interest or pleasure, plus changes in sleep, appetite and energy.

questions.q: Unipolar depression differs from bipolar disorder because unipolar involves:
options: Only depressive low mood, without mania
questions.explain: Unipolar depression involves low mood only, whereas bipolar disorder alternates between depression and mania.

questions.q: Which manual is used to help diagnose depression by listing symptoms and criteria?
questions.explain: Depression can be diagnosed using classification systems such as the ICD, which set out symptoms and criteria.

questions.q: The biological explanation links depression to low levels of which neurotransmitter?
questions.explain: The biological explanation suggests low serotonin activity at synapses is linked to the low mood seen in depression.

questions.q: Evidence that depression can run in families is used to support which explanation?
questions.explain: A genetic influence, shown by depression running in families, supports the biological explanation.

questions.q: Beck's cognitive theory explains depression using the 'negative triad', which is negative views about:
options: The self, the world and the future
questions.explain: Beck's negative triad involves negative thoughts about the self, the world and the future, maintaining depression.

questions.q: A person with a negative self-schema, according to the cognitive explanation, will tend to:
questions.explain: A negative self-schema leads people to interpret information about themselves in a negative, biased way.

questions.q: A student fails one test and concludes 'I'm useless and always will be.' This faulty thinking best fits:
questions.explain: Overgeneralising from one event reflects faulty, irrational thinking central to the cognitive explanation of depression.

questions.q: The main aim of CBT for depression is to:
options: Identify and challenge negative, irrational thoughts and change behaviour
questions.explain: CBT works by identifying and challenging negative, irrational thoughts and encouraging more helpful behaviour.

questions.q: Which is a strength of CBT compared with drug therapy for depression?
options: It tackles the causes of faulty thinking, not just symptoms
It gives instant relief in minutes
It requires no effort from the patient
questions.explain: CBT addresses the underlying negative thinking rather than only masking symptoms, and effects can be longer-lasting.

questions.q: Antidepressant drugs such as SSRIs mainly work by:
options: Increasing the availability of serotonin at the synapse
questions.explain: SSRIs increase serotonin available in the synapse, which can help lift mood in depression.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of using drug therapy for depression?
options: It challenges irrational thoughts too well
It can have side effects and may treat symptoms rather than causes
questions.explain: Drugs can cause side effects and tend to treat symptoms rather than the underlying causes of depression.

questions.q: Which is a psychological explanation of addiction in the AQA specification?
questions.explain: Peer influence is a psychological/social explanation; addiction is also explained through learning and genetic factors.

questions.q: A teenager starts smoking because their friends do and it makes them feel accepted. This best fits:
questions.explain: Starting a behaviour to fit in with friends reflects peer influence, a psychological explanation of addiction.

questions.q: Aversion therapy treats addiction by:
options: Pairing the addictive behaviour with an unpleasant response
questions.explain: Aversion therapy pairs the unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus so it becomes associated with discomfort.

questions.q: A person attends a self-help group where members support each other to stay drug-free. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Self-help groups use peer support and shared experience to help people overcome addiction.
